1. # **Introduction**  {#introduction}

We were tasked with creating a Radio Teletype (RTTY) system. RTTY is a wireless form of telegraph that uses radio frequencies to communicate. In place of radio frequencies, we used an infrared LED for our transmitter and a photodiode for our receiver. The LED pulses at two different frequencies that are encoded to be the mark and space. The receiver circuit converts the current from the photodiode into a voltage. This signal is filtered through two different signal paths, which are compared to distinguish its frequency. This is decoded by our receiver arduino to determine if it is receiving a mark or a space. The receiver detects groups of marks and spaces as UART packets, which it interprets as ASCII characters to recreate the transmitted message.

2. # **High Level Design** {#high-level-design}

	Below is a high level diagram of our project followed by a more detailed block diagram of each stage.  
![][image1]  
Figure 1: High level system diagram

![][image2]  
Figure 2: Transmitter block diagram.  
![][image3]  
Figure 3: Receiver block diagram.

		The block diagram shows the path of the signal from the ASCII message all the way to the user output. The transmitter uses code to control the transmission of two different frequencies of pulsinging infrared light. The photodiode in the receiver circuit generates current that is proportional to the amount of infrared light it detects. The transimpedance amplifier converts this generated current into a voltage signal for further processing. This signal is passed through a bandpass to eliminate DC offset and noise. The amplifier increases the amplitude of the voltage signal. The signal is fed to two separate bandpass filters to isolate the mark frequency and space frequency. The rectifiers take the two signals and make any negative voltages positive. The comparator then determines which frequency has a greater amplitude. Depending on which is greater, a logic high or a logic low is sent to the arduino. The arduino code then interprets each packet back into ASCII, displaying it on the console. 

3. # **Transmitter Circuit** {#transmitter-circuit}

	The transmitter uses a simple circuit and well-designed code to transmit the mark and   
space frequencies within \+/- 2Hz of the specified values. The first arduino presented issues, so it was replaced with a spare arduino board. The new arduino board outputs 3.3V, so a 2.1kΩ current limiting resistor was chosen to achieve exactly the specified limit of 1mA. The circuit can be seen below.  
![][image4]  
Figure 4: Transmitter circuit with infrared LED

4. # **Transmitter Code** {#transmitter-code}

The code for the transmitter converts ascii characters into binary packets. It then sends a pulsing signal to the IR LED with a frequency determined by the bits of the packet. It checks to make sure the new frequency is different before setting the frequency output, because each time it is set it causes noise in the signal. The data is transmitted using the UART data frame with one start bit, eight data bits, and one stop bit. It is transmitted at a baud rate of 45.45. The state diagram can be seen below.  
**![][image5]**  
Figure 5: State diagram for transmitter code.

5. # **Receiver Subsystem \- Transimpedance Amplifier** {#receiver-subsystem---transimpedance-amplifier}

	A transimpedance amplifier is used to convert the small current from the photodiode into a voltage. This voltage is what will be processed by the rest of the circuit to determine the received frequency. It is composed of an op amp and resistors. The gain is controlled by its feedback resistance. The equations, simulation, and output voltage measurements can be seen below.  
The output voltage can be determined by the following equation:   
Vout \=RI  
	Where R is the feedback resistance and I is the current generated by the photodiode.

7. # **Receiver Subsystem \- Filters** {#receiver-subsystem---filters}

	Active filters are used to attenuate the signal at all frequencies other than the mark and space frequencies. The signal coming out of the amplifier is fed to two different filters, creating two signal paths. The filters each have a center frequency within 5Hz of the specified mark or space frequency. The attenuation difference between the two frequencies is 15 dB. This large difference makes it easier to distinguish between the two, increasing performance. The general circuit schematic for each filter stage can be seen below. Note for the governing equation that the capacitance of the two capacitors is equal.

8. # **Receiver Subsystem \- Rectifier** {#receiver-subsystem---rectifier}

The two signals are passed through a full wave rectifier so they are fully positive before being input to the comparator circuit. This ensures that the comparator can compare the amplitude of the two signals. The simulation of the rectifier can be seen below.   
![][image29]  
Figure 27: Rectifier simulated in LTSpice  
As seen in the following simulation traces, when given a 3V sinusoidal input, the rectifier essentially inverts the negative half of the signal, making the entire wave positive.  
![][image30]  
Figure 28: rectifier simulation. Input in green and output in blue, cursors show lowest point for each.  
![][image31]  
Figure 29: Full wave rectifiers for each signal path.

![][image32]

Figure 30: Rectifier waveforms measured using AD3

The output of the simulated rectifier matches the physical output, validating the design.

9. # **Receiver Subsystem \- Comparator** {#receiver-subsystem---comparator}

	A comparator circuit is used to detect which frequency has a higher amplitude. When the mark frequency signal has a higher amplitude, the comparator system outputs a logic high utilizing the pull-up resistor. When the space frequency amplitude is higher, the comparator system outputs a logic low, which is tied to ground. This signal is sent directly to the arduino to be interpreted by code. The physical comparator circuit can be seen below.

10. # **Receiver Code** {#receiver-code}

	The code for the receiver receives the output of the comparator and samples it to recreate UART data packets. It waits for the start of a packet, and then begins reading the bits.  
As an extra step to prevent false starts, it makes sure the start bit is correct before it reads a packet. It uses an average of 100 analog samples to determine whether the bit is a mark or a space. It then interprets groups of packets into ascii characters. The state diagram of the code can be seen below. 

**![][image39]**  
Figure 36: State diagram of receiver code.

12. **Modification**

A 10uF and 0.1uF were added to the power rails of the breadboard. They help to reduce noise caused from external sources, like laptop chargers, which we found were creating interference. 

13. **Overall System Results**

The system works reliably at a distance of up to 30ft. It can also operate at close distances down to 6 inches by adjusting the comparator reference potentiometer. 

14. **Future Work**

We would like to expand the capability of our design by connecting a radio antenna to receive real RTTY messages. It would also be interesting to increase the LED power to communicate over longer distances. It is also a future goal to make the system have user input for the transmitter, and possibly make the communication bidirectional. 

15. **Conclusion**

	We have produced an exceptional circuit with exceptional results. We learned a lot about how signals degrade over distance, as well as the challenges of separating the signal from the noise floor. We also learned a huge amount about designing filters to use available component values to greatly reduce circuit complexity. If we were to start this project again, we would start with a simpler design first to make prototyping and testing quicker. Additionally, we would like to try using low noise op amps for the first stages instead of low power op amps. Overall, we gained a lot of knowledge and experience working with analog signals and filtering.

Receiver code:  
\#define baudDelay 11 //adjusted from 22  
\#define DATAPIN A0  
\#define INDICATOR\_PIN 10  
\#define SAMPLES 100  
\#define SAMPLE\_DELAY 5  
//Elori Smile

void setup() {  
  pinMode(LED\_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);  
  pinMode(INDICATOR\_PIN, OUTPUT);  
  pinMode(11, OUTPUT);  
  Serial.begin (9600);  
  Serial.println("\\n......\\n");  
}

void loop() {  
  if (\!readBit(3)) {  
    digitalWrite(LED\_BUILTIN, HIGH);  
    //Serial.println("T");  
    readPacket();  
  }  
  else {  
    digitalWrite(LED\_BUILTIN, LOW);  
  }  
  //delay(4\*baudDelay);  
    
}

void readPacket() {  
  byte parityBit \= 0; //0 for even bit parity, 1 for odd bit parity  
  if (readBit(50)) {  
    return;  
  }  
  delay(baudDelay+7);  
  unsigned char packet \= 0;  
  for (int i=0; i\<8; i++) {  
    digitalWrite(11, HIGH);  
    bool bitstate \= readBit(100);  
    packet \+= bitstate \<\< i;  
    parityBit ^= bitstate;  
    digitalWrite(INDICATOR\_PIN, \!bitstate);  
    digitalWrite(11, LOW);  
    //Serial.print(bitstate);  
    delay(baudDelay);  
    delayMicroseconds(500);  
  }  
  byte parityCheck \= readBit(100);

  delay(7\*baudDelay);  
    
  //Serial.print(packet, BIN);  
  //Serial.print("|");  
  //Serial.print(packet, HEX);  
  //Serial.print("|");  
  //Serial.print(parityBit);  
  Serial.print(char(packet));  
  return packet;

  if (parityBit \== parityCheck) {  
    Serial.print(char(packet));  
    return packet;  
  }  
  else {  
    //Serial.println("Packet error");  
    return NULL;  
  }  
}

bool readBit(int samples) {  
  unsigned long data\_sum;  
  for(int i=0; i\<samples; i++) {   
    data\_sum \+= analogRead(DATAPIN);  
    //delayMicroseconds(SAMPLE\_DELAY-1);  
  }  
  bool bitState \= (data\_sum/samples \> 500);  
  //bool bitState \= ((analogRead(DATAPIN)+analogRead(DATAPIN)+analogRead(DATAPIN)+analogRead(DATAPIN)+analogRead(DATAPIN)+analogRead(DATAPIN)) \> 5000);  
  //delay(baudDelay);  
  //bool bitState \= digitalRead(A0);  
  return \!bitState;  
}
